pages.text: Some friends talk a lot. Some friends talk a little. Loki was a talk-a-little friend, and Azi liked that just fine. Loki's whole name was Lokjit. Azi's whole name was Azad. But big names are for grown-up days. Friends use the small, soft ones.

They ate pizza at the table by the big window, the way they always did. Loki laughed his whole-face laugh — the one where his eyes closed and his shoulders went up — and Azi laughed because Loki was laughing, and soon nobody even remembered what was funny. That is the best kind of laughing.

Then Loki got quiet. Quieter than usual, even for Loki. "My family is moving," he said. "To China. We are going to live near my nǎinai and my yéye. My grandma and my grandpa. They miss us very, very much."
"Is China far?" asked Azi. "So far you have to sleep on the airplane," said Loki. "You wake up, and you are still flying."
Azi looked down at his pizza. It suddenly didn't taste like anything at all.
That night, Azi was quiet at dinner. Quiet in the bath. Quiet all the way into pajamas. Papa brought the globe to Azi's room and gave it a slow spin.

"We are here," said Papa, touching a tiny dot. "And look — Dada and Dadi are here, in Howell. So close, one finger can touch us both at the same time." Azi put his finger on both places at once. It was easy.

"Lito and Lita are here," said Papa, turning the globe. "In Colombia. Far — that's why their hugs come through the computer." Then Papa turned the globe almost all the way around. "And China is here."
In between was blue, and more blue, and more blue after that. Azi's chest felt tight and wobbly at the same time, like a tower of blocks right before it tips.
"Loki can just live in my house," said Azi. "We have room." Papa smiled a sad smile. "You wish he could stay." "Yes." "Me too."
They sat with the wobbly feeling together for a while, because some feelings just need company.

Then Papa said, "Azi. You know how Lito and Lita live far away? How their faces come to us through the screen? How Mama misses them so much?" Azi nodded. He knew that missing. It lived at their house too.
"Loki's nǎinai has been missing Loki just like that. Every single day. And now —" Papa turned the globe gently — "she gets to have him close. The way we have Dada and Dadi close."
Azi thought about Dada and Dadi's house. The samosas. The Hess trucks. The hugs that smelled like home cooking.
"Does his nǎinai make him snacks?" Azi asked. "I bet she has been saving up snacks," said Papa. "And hugs. Years and years of hugs."
Azi was quiet. It was still sad. But now the sad made sense — the way a puzzle piece makes sense when you finally see where it goes.

Then Papa stretched his arms out wide. Wider. As wide as they would go. "My love for you goes from here... to here," said Papa. "And if you flew to the moon, it would stretch all the way there without breaking. That's what love does. It stretches."
"Even across the whole ocean?" "Especially across the whole ocean."
Before moving day, Loki came over one more time. They sat on the circular rug in the playroom, and Loki took out his special paper — the kind that folds crisp and remembers every crease.
"We will make birds," said Loki. "Two. One for you. One for me." Loki folded slowly. Fold... press... breathe out slow. "Slow folds make strong birds," he said.
Azi tried. His folds went a little crooked. "Good," said Loki, in his noticing voice. "Crooked wings have more adventure in them."
When they finished, two paper birds sat side by side on the rug. They matched — almost. One flew a little straighter. One flew a little wilder.

"Your bird stays with you," said Loki. "My bird comes with me to China." "How do they work?" asked Azi. "When you hold yours, you think of me," said Loki. "When I hold mine, I think of you. That's how they remember."
Then Loki got quiet. Quieter than the paper. "My nǎinai I know," he said. "But the kids there... the kids will be all new." His voice sounded like a very small fold.
Azi thought hard. Then he reached for his guitar — it was always within reach — and played his three chords, the ones he played when he was figuring things out. C... G... Am.
"When everything feels too new," said Azi, "hum this. It's from my house." Loki hummed it back. A little crooked. The good kind.
On the last day, there were hugs. There are always hugs on last days. Loki looked up at the sky, the way he did when he was about to notice something.
"In Chinese, we don't say goodbye," he said. "We say zàijiàn. Zài means again. Jiàn means see. See-again." "Zàijiàn," said Azi, holding the word carefully, like folded paper.
"And Azi — at night, look at the moon. I will look too. It is the same moon. It shines on Rahway, and it shines on China, and it never forgets anybody."
One more hug. The kind you remember. "Zàijiàn, Azi." "Zàijiàn, Loki."
The next week, the bus felt different. The seat where Loki used to fold his paper was just a seat now. The wobbly feeling came back, bigger this time. It sat right in the middle of Azi's chest.
So Azi got paper, and he tried to fold a bird. The first one crumpled. It looked more like a hat. The second one folded wrong. It looked more like a puddle. Then Azi remembered. Slow.
Fold... press... breathe out slow. Fold... press... breathe out slow.
The third bird came out crooked. The good kind.

And then, one Saturday, the laptop opened like a window — and there was Loki! His hair was the same. His laugh was the same. On the windowsill behind him, in his new room in China, sat a small paper bird.
"Your bird made it!" said Azi. "Birds remember," said Loki. And then, from the other side of the whole world, Loki hummed three notes Azi knew by heart. C... G... Am. A little crooked. The good kind.
They giggled the no-reason giggle until both their shoulders went up. "Next call," said Papa, "pizza on both sides of the world."
When the screen closed, Azi felt sunshine and a little rain, both at the same time. "Seeing Loki is sunshine," said Mama. "Missing him is a little rain. Both can be true at the same time, mi amor."
That night, Azi put his paper bird on the windowsill, facing the moon. Pandies watched from the shelf and said nothing, which is how Pandies says everything.
The moon was big and round and quiet. It shone on the Westfield. It shone on the garden.
It shone on Dada and Dadi's house in Howell, and on Lito and Lita's house in Colombia.
And far, far away, over the whole blue ocean, it was shining on Loki — and on his nǎinai, who finally had her boy close.
Azi stretched his arms out wide. Wider. As wide as they would go. "Zàijiàn, Loki," he whispered.
Mama tucked the blanket up to his chin. "Sleep, mi cielo." Azi closed his eyes.
Missing is what love does when a friend is far away. It stretches — across streets, across oceans, all the way to China.
And love that stretches does not break.
Same moon. Same birds. Same friends. Zàijiàn.

a little bit bent instead of perfectly straight
squished into a wrinkly ball, like paper in your fist
a little round Earth you can spin with your finger
the little shelf under the glass where small things sit and look outside
a Chinese word for goodbye that secretly means 'see you again'
